newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan factions stalemated at pass north of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Afghan factions stalemated at pass north of Kabul.

text.p: Commanders with ousted Afghan government forces said on Thursday that a large offensive the previous day had so far failed to budge Taleban militia from the strategic De Sabz pass north of Kabul.
"We are in the same positions we were last night," Najim Khan, one commander, told reporters.

Led by Ahmad Shah Masood, military chief in the ousted government of President Burhannuddin Rabbni, anti-Taleban forces are trying to dislodge the purist Islamic movement from the Afghan capital Kabul.
The Taleban took Kabul at the end of last month, giving it control of some two-thirds of the country.
On Wednesday, fighters of the mainly Tajik Jamiat-i-Islami faction unleashed a large attack on the Taleban in an attempt to take the De Sabz pass, which lies 10 km (six miles) from Kabul.
The road from Masood-controlled territory into northeast Kabul cuts through the pass and would give ousted government forces command over heights vital to an advance on the capital.

The front was quiet on Thursday except for a few shells fired by the Taleban onto Masood's positions below another pass, Khair Khana, around 15 km (nine miles) north of Kabul, and a bombing raid on the village of Kalakan at 09.15 a.m. (0445 GMT).
Three houses were hit in the raid and women and children fled the village while men tried frantically to dig bodies out of the rubble.
A reporter with the British Broadcasting Corporation who visited Kalakan later in the day said 14 bodies, mostly of women and children, had been recovered.
There has been heavy fighting north of Kabul during days of ceasefire talks being pressed by Pakistani Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar and U.N. Special Envoy Norbert Holl.

Holl saw northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum in his stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif on Wednesday and planned to fly to Kandahar, headquarters of the purist Taleban movement, for further talks on Thursday.

But his hopes of arranging a ceasefire were viewed as slim, with Dostum and his ally, Masood, demanding the demilitarisation of Kabul. The Taleban, whose fighters captured Kabul on September 27, have rejected this as unacceptable.
"Success is far from being guaranteed," Holl said after talking to Dostum.
